title: Parker's greatest blues at a San Pedro dive
summary: At a Saturday jam in a blues joint, Parker sat on a 4-by-4 seat and played the greatest blues Edwards heard from him.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: But anyway, we used to play at different places. But I never will forget one setting, one Saturday. There was a bass player around here named Shifty Henry. In fact, he wrote one of the tunes that Earl Coleman recorded when he recorded with Erroll Garner and Charlie Parker on that Dial date...

Anyway, he was working at a club on San Pedro and Vernon. And it was a stone dive, a real Blues joint, you know! Hah-hah-hah-hah! So they used to have jam sessions there on Saturday afternoons. And so Charlie had been over to the house, and so we were going to go down to the set. We walked over there, in fact. And when we walked in the door, they were playing the blues, and they had a real nice thing going. And he could get the saxophone out of that bag quicker than anybody you've ever seen in your life. Almost like magician he could get it out when he was getting to play, he could get it out so fast, you know. And he headed straight for the bandstand. I can see the picture plain as I can see your face now. He sat on this 4-by-4 seat, and the bandstand was about 6 or 8 inches high, and he let his feet hang off the bandstand (they had a dance floor), and he had his horn in between his legs. And he played... I think that's the greatest Blues I ever heard him play, when he played the Blues that afternoon in this place, you know. It was really something. It was classic, you know.
I had so many classic moments with him, in different places, different situations, you know.
